passage: As their neighbour, I can see the veranda of the old house where Jomon and Jagdish grew up, and this spring they sat there many Sunday afternoons with papers and a calculator. At first I heard raised voices, one wanting the house sold, one wanting to keep it. Then Jomon wrote something on a pad and read it out: one of them could buy the other out over five years. Jagdish said, "Or we rent it and share what comes in." They started drawing columns for each idea. I couldn't hear all of it. I don't know whether either was truly happy about giving something up. But the shouting stopped, and the pad filled with options. Last week I saw them shake hands, and neither looked like the loser.

qa.q: What two options ended up on the pad?
qa.a: One of them buying the other out over five years, or renting the house and sharing what comes in.

qa.q: What might Jagdish have felt about giving something up, according to the neighbour?
qa.a: The neighbour cannot be sure, but Jagdish may have felt torn or reluctant, since the neighbour says not knowing if either was truly happy.

qa.q: What could Jomon and Jagdish do to make either option work?
qa.a: They could agree on amounts, dates and who handles repairs for whichever option they choose, and have it written down.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see the change over the spring?
qa.a: The neighbour sees the shouting stop and the pad fill with options, ending with a handshake where neither looked like the loser.

grounding: Instead of one side taking everything, Jomon and Jagdish consider a buyout over time or renting the property and sharing income.

subtype: Approach: win-win options such as buyout or rotation [Thinking]
passage:
Sunday, 2 February. Mridul and his brother Anirban sit on the roof of their late mother's house in Siliguri, stuck. Anirban wants to live in it; Mridul, who works in Pune, wants his share. "So one of us loses," Anirban says.
Wednesday, 5 February. On the train back, Mridul keeps turning it over. Why does it have to be all or nothing? He types two ideas into his phone. One: Anirban buys my half slowly, over years, from what he'd otherwise pay in rent. Two: we rent the house out and split the income until one of us is ready.
Saturday, 15 February. On a video call he reads both out. Anirban is quiet, then says, "The slow buyout. I could do that." They agree to ask a lawyer how to put it in writing.

qa.a: Anirban buys his half slowly over years, or they rent the house out and split the income until one of them is ready.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when he said "So one of us loses"?
qa.a: He felt stuck and resigned, seeing only an all-or-nothing choice.

qa.q: Why might the slow buyout suit both brothers?
qa.a: Anirban keeps the home and Mridul still receives his share, just spread over time.

qa.q: What would have changed if Mridul had not questioned the all-or-nothing idea?
qa.a: The brothers would likely still be stuck on the roof, with one of them feeling he had lost.

grounding: It shows a brother thinking past keep-or-sell to a gradual buyout or renting and sharing income, which widens what a fair deal can be.

passage:
Irfan sir leaned back in the staff room when the young clerk mentioned fighting with his brother over their father's flat. "Let me tell you about Elizabeth, who sat at that desk before you. When she was about twenty-five, she and her two brothers inherited their parents' cottage in Kodaikanal. One brother wanted to sell; she wanted to keep it; the other just wanted peace. They argued for a year.
Then one evening she came to me with a sheet of paper scribbled all over. 'What if it isn't keep or sell?' she said. She had two ideas. She could buy her brothers' shares slowly, a little every year. Or they could rent it to holidaymakers and split the income until someone was ready to decide. The brothers chose renting.
The cottage is still in the family. What I remember is that she stopped asking who wins and started asking what else was possible."

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she came to Irfan with the scribbled sheet?
qa.a: She was likely hopeful and excited, having found a way out of a year of arguing.

qa.q: Which choice in the story opened a way forward, and why?
qa.a: Elizabeth asking "What if it isn't keep or sell?", because it produced a slow buyout and a rental option that could suit all three siblings.

qa.q: How might the brother who just wanted peace have felt about renting?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved, since renting ended the fighting without forcing anyone to lose.

grounding: It shows a young woman thinking beyond keep-or-sell to a gradual buyout or a shared rental income, expanding what a fair deal could be.
